preamble: A voiceless aspirated bilabial stop [pʰ] corresponding to, or becoming, a voiced stop [b]. The one well-known case is Ancient Macedonian, where Plutarch reports that Macedonians said Bilippos for Philippos and Beronikē for Pherenikē, and Aristophanes' bird name κεβλήπυρις 'red-cap' shows β where Attic κεφαλή 'head' has φ. The direction of the change is disputed: on the traditional comparative view Macedonian β continues Proto-Indo-European *bʰ directly (*bʰ > b, parallel to δάνος 'death' beside θάνατος < *dʰenh₂-), so the relevant cell is bʱ → b; on the view now favoured by many specialists (Brixhe, Crespo, Hatzopoulos), Macedonian is a Greek dialect and the voiced stops arose by secondary voicing of the common Greek aspirates, i.e. pʰ > b. Outside Macedonian this exact change is rare.

examples.note: Plutarch, Greek Questions 9 (Moralia 292e): Delphians use b in place of p, 'not in place of ph, as Macedonians do who say Bilip and balacros and Beronikē'.
The Macedonian form of the name spread through the Ptolemaic dynasty; Attic keeps φ.
First element κεβλή 'head', with a Macedonian-style voiced stop where common Greek κεφαλή has the aspirate φ; Wiktionary glosses the bird as the firecrest.

sources: Plutarch. Quaestiones Graecae 9 (Moralia 292e). In Babbitt, F. C. (trans.) (1936). Plutarch, Moralia IV. Loeb Classical Library 305. Harvard University Press. https://catalog.perseus.org/catalog/urn:cts:greekLit:tlg0007.tlg084b
